pairs.rationale: Mary's rising and going to Judah's hill country is compared, cautiously, with David and the people's rising and going on an ascent to bring the ark from a house on a hill. The larger visitation narrative supplies the household and blessing setting. This is a possible journey-pattern echo; Samuel's Judah wording concerns its rulers, and neither an identical route or city nor an identification of Mary with the ark follows.

Elizabeth later explicitly recalls the sound of Mary's greeting entering her ears and the infant leaping with gladness. That speech refers back to the greeting narrated here at Zechariah's house. This is an internal action-and-recollection link within one visit, not a separate witness or evidence for words of the greeting that Luke does not record.

The relatives object that the proposed name John has no family precedent; the earlier angelic instruction explicitly tells Zechariah to name the child John. The comparison explains the narrative contrast between family expectation and the announced name without identifying other people named John as relatives or treating the objection as independent proof of the angel's appearance.

Luke dates this first registration by Quirinius's governing Syria; Acts places Judas the Galilean's uprising in the days of the registration. These are concrete registration notices in Luke and Acts. Acts does not name Quirinius or Augustus here, so this link alone neither establishes that the registrations are identical nor resolves Luke's chronology.

The shepherds decide to go see the announced birth after the angels depart; Matthew's visitors follow the star and enter to see the Child with Mary. Both narratives connect heavenly guidance with going to see Jesus as a child. The shepherds and magi, the guiding signs, the locations described, and the actions are distinct; no simultaneous arrival is inferred.

Luke identifies Anna as a prophetess in the Jerusalem temple scene; Kings identifies Olda as a prophetess living in Jerusalem and names her household connections. This compares specifically named female prophetic figures associated with Jerusalem. Olda is not Anna, and Kings supplies no confirmation of Anna's father, tribe, age, or marriage history.

The family's customary festival journey, at Jesus' age of twelve, is compared with the law's recurring festival obligations, including unleavened bread and male appearance before the Lord. This supplies scriptural background to the festival custom identified as Passover in Luke's preceding verse. Exodus gives no age-twelve rule or later initiation custom.

In Luke the parents return while the boy remains in Jerusalem without their knowledge; in Samuel the family departs for Armathaim while the child remains ministering before the Lord with Eli. Both scenes distinguish a child's remaining at the place of worship from the household's departure. Samuel's stay is deliberate dedication, unlike Luke's unrecognized separation.

The dating notice names Pilate over Judea and Herod as Galilee's tetrarch. Later Pilate asks whether Jesus is Galilean and sends Him to Herod on learning that He belongs to Herod's jurisdiction. The later scene illuminates those particular jurisdictional roles; it does not verify the Tiberius-year date or the other rulers and territories in the earlier list.

The physician-heal-yourself proverb anticipates a demand that Jesus demonstrate at home the works heard of elsewhere. At the cross the mockers similarly contrast His saving others with an alleged inability to save Himself. This compares the challenge to prove power on one's own behalf, with hometown demands and crucifixion mockery kept distinct; neither proverb nor mockery is endorsed as true.

The synagogue becomes angry after Jesus' examples of aid to the Sidonian widow and the Syrian Naaman; Acts' crowd turns against Paul at the reported commission to Gentiles. Both scenes place a hostile response after speech about God's activity beyond Israel. The speakers, audiences, and occasions differ, and this does not reduce every listener's motives to an unstated explanation.

Luke's crowd takes Jesus outside the city and toward a hill to hurl Him down; Acts' crowd rushes Stephen and drives him outside the city to stone him. The concrete pattern is hostile collective expulsion for lethal violence. The persons, cities, methods, and outcomes differ; Stephen's stoning does not establish that Jesus was thrown from the hill.

Luke says Jesus passes through the hostile crowd and departs; John says those seeking to seize Him do not retain Him and He goes out from their hand. These are distinct narrated escapes from hostile attempts to take Him. John does not reproduce the hilltop method, and neither account is used to add a miraculous mechanism or an identical occasion to the other.

Luke introduces fishermen's boats and nets being washed before Jesus' call; Mark introduces James and John in a boat putting the nets in order before their call. This compares fishing-work settings around the disciples' calling, while retaining washing versus putting in order and Luke's fishermen outside the boats versus Mark's named men in a boat.

Both Jesus-directed catches produce so many fish that coordinated handling becomes necessary: Luke's partners bring the other boat and both boats become dangerously loaded, while John's disciples cannot draw the net and the others come in the little boat dragging it. John's scene is after the resurrection and says nothing about two boats sinking; the catches and handling sequences remain distinct.

Luke's elders commend their centurion's love for the nation and construction of their synagogue. Acts identifies Cornelius as a centurion who gives many alms to the people and prays continually. These are specific depictions of centurions' benefaction toward the people, not identification of the two men; Acts does not say Cornelius built Luke's synagogue.

Jesus' journey to Nain introduces the following encounter with a widow whose son is restored; Elijah's journey to Zarephath brings him to a widow at the city gateway, before the later restoration of her son. This compares the opening movements in the wider widow-and-son narratives. The towns, time before the son's death, accompanying crowds, and manner of restoration are not equated.

The woman's repeated kisses of Jesus' feet are contrasted with Simon's omitted greeting kiss in this scene; Judas later approaches Jesus for a kiss and Jesus questions handing over the Son of Man with a kiss. These are contrasting uses of a kiss in Luke, devotion and hospitality versus betrayal, not the same kind of kiss, person, or incident.

The parable begins with a stripped, wounded traveler going toward Jericho; Chronicles describes naked, weakened captives being clothed, helped onto animals, and brought to Jericho. The wider mercy scenes share exposed vulnerability, aid, and Jericho, while the source of harm differs: robbery in Luke, captivity after war in Chronicles. No captive is identified as the parable's traveler.

The priest sees a half-dead traveler on the road and passes by. Deuteronomy forbids seeing a brother's fallen donkey or calf in the way and disregarding it, requiring help instead. The law's explicit seeing-and-not-disregarding instruction supplies a bounded ethical contrast to passing the injured man; the animals and man are distinct, and no purity motive or knowledge of the priest's resources is invented.

The Levite sees the injured traveler and passes by, whereas Proverbs commands rescue of people facing death and rejects ignorance of the person as an adequate excuse before God. This compares failure to aid a person in mortal need with the rescue instruction. Proverbs' people are being led to death, not victims of the same robbery; Luke does not state the Levite's motive.

The Samaritan personally guarantees repayment of further costs incurred caring for the injured man; Paul personally offers to have another's wrong or debt charged to him and promises repayment. The concrete connection is assuming another person's financial burden by an explicit repayment pledge. Innkeeper expenses and the possible debt concerning Onesimus differ, and neither pledge determines the other's amount.

The friend-at-midnight story opens with a person asking another for needed help, and Luke11:8 explains persistence; the widow repeatedly petitions a judge who eventually responds because she troubles him. Both parables use persistent human requests in teaching about prayer. Friendship, bread, midnight and hospitality differ from an unjust judge and a demand for justice; God is not thereby identified as unwilling or unjust.

Luke's traveler arrives at his friend's home, whose host has no food to offer; in Genesis evening travelers are invited into Lot's house and he prepares a feast and unleavened bread for them. This compares the concrete responsibility of receiving travelers with food and shelter. Lot's angelic visitors and available provision are not inserted into Luke's friend or his lack of bread.

The man inside initially refuses the midnight request, invoking the shut door and children in bed; Luke's judge is initially unwilling but later yields to the widow's repeated troubling. With Luke 11:8 supplying the first story's eventual response, the comparison concerns resistance overcome by persistence. Household inconvenience and the judge's stated character are different reasons, not proof that the friend is the same unjust figure.

An expert in the Law tells Jesus that His rebuke insults his group; Matthew's disciples report that the Pharisees stumbled at His saying in a dispute that also begins with handwashing traditions. This compares religious interlocutors' adverse reception of Jesus' purity-related correction. The reporter, wording, teaching sequence and occasion differ; the passages do not independently reproduce the same objection.

Both parables give an economic protagonist's private deliberation in the form 'What shall I do?' followed by the difficulty he faces and a plan. The rich man has too much produce to store, while the steward is losing his position and fears digging or begging. This is a specific repeated monologue pattern, not the same predicament or a common approval of the plans.

Luke's rich man plans larger storehouses to gather abundant grain and his goods; Genesis describes abundant years and Joseph gathering their food into the cities. The concrete comparison is organized grain storage after agricultural abundance. Joseph's preceding plan preserves the land through famine, unlike the rich man's self-directed security; Genesis supplies neither demolition of barns nor Luke's promised years of personal ease.

Jesus' question challenges the assumption that the Siloam victims were greater debtors than their neighbors; John's disciples ask whose sin caused a man's congenital blindness, and Jesus rejects their proposed individual-or-parental explanation. Both passages resist a simple inference from suffering to exceptional personal guilt. John does not attest the tower deaths, and neither passage declares everyone morally sinless.

The later saying explicitly returns to this woman and the same eighteen years, describing her as a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound and whose bond ought to be released. It interprets the earlier spirit of weakness within this particular healing controversy. This is an internal explanatory reference, not an independent diagnosis or a rule that every chronic illness has the same cause.

Jesus pronounces the woman released from her weakness; His earlier synagogue proclamation announces release to captives and to the oppressed. The following Sabbath argument explicitly describes this woman's release from bondage. This is a narrative illustration of the announced release motif, not a claim that every expression in the earlier proclamation denotes this woman's condition or that the pronouncement is a direct quotation.

Both scenes contain an instruction to leave because Herod seeks Jesus' life. Matthew's angel addresses Joseph about the Child and an Egyptian refuge, while Luke records Pharisees warning the adult Jesus, whose reply follows. The life stages, speakers and Herod settings are distinct; the comparison neither identifies the Herods nor establishes that Jesus fled in response to the Pharisees.

Jesus tells messengers to report His healings in both scenes: to John after works including deliverance from evil spirits, and to the ruler described as a fox with a declaration of ongoing exorcisms and healings. The recipient, tone and setting differ. Luke 7 does not explain the fox epithet or the today/tomorrow/third-day completion language, which is not silently equated with a resurrection timetable.

A man with dropsy stands before Jesus during a Sabbath meal under close observation; Mark introduces a man with a withered hand in the synagogue while observers watch for a Sabbath healing to accuse Him. These are specific Sabbath-healing controversy settings with different patients, ailments and venues. Mark does not independently attest dropsy or identify its patient as Luke's man.

Both banquet parables report the result of servants gathering people beyond the original invitees. Luke's slave says the command is fulfilled but room remains, prompting another outreach; Matthew says the wedding feast is filled after gathering people from the roads. This compares the reports and their differing stages, preserving remaining capacity versus fullness rather than replacing Luke's statement with Matthew's.

Luke describes Jesus addressing the great crowd traveling with Him before the cross-bearing demands of discipleship; Mark explicitly calls the crowd together with the disciples to hear self-denial and cross-bearing instruction. The connection is the public audience and introduction to the same costly-following theme. Being already on the road and being summoned are distinct narrative arrangements, not an identical occasion asserted.

The uncompleted building brings spectators' mockery in Luke; Nehemiah records opponents laughing at the Jews' wall building and deriding the wall's strength before a prayer about becoming an object of mockery. This is a concrete construction-and-ridicule comparison. Nehemiah's opponents do not establish an actual abandonment for lack of funds, and their wall is not Luke's tower.

Luke's hypothetical builder begins but cannot finish; Zechariah promises that the hands of Zerubbabel which laid the house's foundation will complete it. The contrast concerns beginning and completing a building, with human cost calculation in Luke and a prophetic assurance in Zechariah. No identical project or general promise to complete every undertaking is inferred.

The father divides property between his sons after the younger requests his share; Deuteronomy regulates a father's assignment of possessions to sons and protects the firstborn's double portion. This is legal background to a paternal inheritance division, not proof of the precise shares or timing in the parable. Luke does not supply the law's two-wives situation or explicitly calculate either son's portion.

Luke places the needy son in work feeding pigs; Leviticus classifies the pig as unclean for Israel and prohibits eating its flesh or touching its carcass. This provides a specific scriptural background for the animal in the scene. It does not turn a dietary and carcass rule into an express prohibition on this employment or assert that the son ate pork.

The hungry son longs to be filled with the pigs' food and receives nothing; the poor man at the rich man's gate longs to be filled with what falls from the table. Both nearby parables depict unfulfilled food longing beside abundance and animals. The pigs eat pods, while the dogs lick sores; Luke does not say the dogs eat the table scraps or identify the two hungry men.

An approaching person hears a celebration and then reacts angrily in each wider scene: Luke's older son hears music and dancing before resenting his brother's welcome; Joshua and Moses hear camp sounds, and Moses sees dancing and becomes angry. The limited narrative comparison preserves a legitimate family celebration versus idolatrous revelry; no idolatry or moral approval of the brother's anger is imported into Luke.

The steward and rich man each reason privately with 'What shall I do?' and name an economic difficulty before proposing a solution. The steward faces removal and inability or reluctance to do other work; the rich man faces crop-storage capacity. The recurring deliberation formula connects the parables without making their circumstances, motives, plans or ensuing evaluations identical.

The steward summons his master's debtors and asks the first what he owes; Matthew's king begins settling accounts and a deeply indebted servant is brought before him. Both parables stage obligations owed to a master through an accounting encounter. The steward is an intermediary, whereas the king is the creditor; debt amounts and the actions that follow are different.

The two consecutive transactions deliberately repeat the debt question and written-document revision while changing commodity and figures: a hundred baths of oil becomes fifty here, and a hundred kors of wheat becomes eighty in the second. This is an internal structural comparison of the steward's dealings. The different reductions do not establish an interest-rate, commission, or legally authorized remission theory.

The wheat transaction repeats the earlier oil debtor's written revision, but changes a hundred to eighty rather than a hundred to fifty. This explicit repeated transaction pattern permits comparison of the different stated reductions without treating the commodities or quantities as identical. No explanation involving removed interest, commission, local prices, or the master's authorization is added.

The formerly feasting rich man asks for water in painful torment while Lazarus is comforted in the surrounding dialogue. Isaiah contrasts the Lord's servants eating, drinking and rejoicing with opponents' hunger, thirst and cries of heart-pain. This is a bounded judgment-and-reversal comparison, not a source for the wet-finger request, flame mechanism, or an identical map of the afterlife.

The fixed chasm prevents movement between torment and Abraham's company; the earlier teaching depicts a closed door, rejected pleas to enter, and people outside seeing Abraham in God's kingdom. Both depict decisive exclusion alongside awareness of Abraham's blessed company. Chasm and doorway remain different images, with no claim that the scenes give identical geography or add a later crossing possibility.

The rich man wants his living brothers solemnly warned so they may avoid torment; Ezekiel's watchman must convey God's warning so a lawless hearer may turn and live rather than die. The connection is warning before destructive judgment with an opportunity to change. Ezekiel neither identifies the five brothers nor authorizes a visit from the dead; the following Luke dialogue instead points to Moses and the Prophets.

deferred.reason: The delay and the people's wondering were reread with the announcement and muteness that explain this scene. The priestly division regulations in 1 Chronicles 24 do not describe a comparable waiting crowd or duration of delay. No generic wait for a religious leader is retained.

The fixed priestly ministry background in 1 Chronicles 24:19 was considered, but it gives no particular completed term or return home corresponding to this transition. It informs the earlier division setting more directly than this departure, so the unit remains unpaired.

Acts 5:37 provides a registration-related dating notice, compared separately with Luke 2:2, but it gives neither Augustus's decree nor this inhabited-world scope. No imperial decree, synchronism, or identical census is supplied for this unit.

The registration notices in Acts 5:37 and the neighboring Luke verses do not reproduce everyone traveling to an own city. General census language would not illuminate this distinctive procedure, and no external administrative rule or ancestral-city requirement is added.

David tending a flock in the Bethlehem setting of 1 Samuel 16 was considered. It does not share the nighttime field watch, the group of shepherds, or the angelic setting. A broad shepherd association alone is not retained for this narrative unit.

The John-birth report and local reaction in Luke 1:63–66 were reconsidered. They share social response to an unusual birth but not the shepherds' testimony, and wonder alone adds too little as a fresh connection. The unit remains deferred.

The parents' later response and failure to understand in Luke 2:48–50 were compared with this wonder at Simeon's words. Wonder is not itself lack of understanding, and the later exchange does not independently illuminate this particular testimony or parental response.

The neighboring discovery story and Luke's lost-and-found parables were reconsidered. They do not reproduce the mistaken traveling-company assumption, day's journey, or search among relatives. No allegory about Jesus being morally lost or an identical later search is retained.

The continued search and return to Jerusalem were reread with the discovery in the temple. A generic search-until-found pattern does not supply a concrete separate connection to this return journey. Its specific narrative action stays deferred.

Simeon's earlier sword-to-Mary's-soul saying was considered alongside this anguished parental question. It does not explicitly identify the childhood search as fulfillment, and general maternal pain is insufficient to decide that interpretation. No fulfillment claim or new pair is retained.

Matthew 1:12–16 was reread as a nearby postexilic genealogy candidate. Its chain does not establish Matthat–Levi–Melchi–Jannai–Joseph. Shared or similar names are not sufficient to recover relationships or equate the differently traced lineages.

The reread Matthew lineage does not establish Mattathias–Amos–Nahum–Esli–Naggai. No prophetic-author identity for Amos or Nahum is inferred from a repeated name, and no supplied paternal chain is replaced by a conjectured harmonization.

The actual Maath–Mattathias–Semein–Josech–Joda sequence remains without a matching chain in the reread Matthew genealogy. Similar spellings cannot establish the persons or their relationships; no pair is retained.

No matching Melchi–Addi–Cosam–Elmadam–Er chain was established in the candidate genealogy. An Er elsewhere or the repeated Melchi inside Luke does not establish identity across these generations. The precise lineage remains deferred.

The ancestral Jesus–Eliezer–Jorim–Matthat–Levi sequence was distinguished from Jesus Christ and from other repeated Matthat or Levi names. The reread Matthew chain does not establish these links, so no identity-based target is retained.

The Simeon–Judah–Joseph–Jonam–Eliakim sequence was read against the postexilic Matthew sequence. Neither familiar patriarchal names nor Matthew's differently situated Eliakim establishes the same persons or chain. No lineage harmonization receives credit.

Nehemiah 8:5–8 provides a public Scripture reading and explanation, but has an opened book, standing audience and different actions. That shared setting does not add a specific counterpart to Jesus returning the rolled scroll, sitting, and receiving the synagogue's fixed gaze.

Mark 9:15 places the crowd's astonishment before the afflicted boy's healing, on seeing and greeting Jesus. Luke's response to God's majesty follows the healing and introduces another prediction. The timing and focus are distinct, and generic amazement alone is not retained.

Matthew 10:23's instruction to flee persecution was compared with the Samaritan village's refusal and Jesus' subsequent departure. Luke does not describe flight from persecution here or reproduce the instruction; no punitive fire or extra departure detail is added.

Deuteronomy 21:15–17 regulates paternal inheritance and the firstborn's portion, but the claimant's birth rank, family structure and legal rights are unspecified. Unlike the father's division scene in Luke 15:12, this request gives no particular basis for applying that provision. It remains deferred.

Psalm 78:1–3 was considered for violent bloodshed and violation of worship. It describes foreign devastation of Jerusalem, not Pilate's Galileans or blood mixed with their sacrifices. The common religious-violence topic is not retained as a sufficiently particular comparison.

Ruth 1:1–6 was read for famine, loss abroad and return toward food. Its famine precedes migration, while Luke's famine follows the son's journey and spending. The shared hardship setting does not add a close connection to this sequence or identify the country, so no pair is retained.

The father's later provision of clothing and a calf feast was compared with the son's thought about hired workers' abundant bread. It answers his deprivation generally but does not repeat the workers' position or this specific realization. No generic bread or hunger link is added.

Luke 18:36–37 also narrates hearing something, asking what it means, and receiving a report. That is a common inquiry pattern with different hearers, sounds and consequences; it offers no stronger substantive connection to the older son's particular servant question.

Job 2:7–8 was read for bodily sores and a sufferer outside an ordinary residential setting. Job's ulcer, its stated cause and dung-heap scene differ from Lazarus's unnamed cause and placement at the rich man's gate. The general afflicted-person resemblance remains too loose for a retained pair.

The proposed visit to the father's house was reread with Abraham's reply and the request's warning purpose. The reply interprets the same dialogue rather than supplying a separate visit, and no actual journey by a dead messenger is inferred. The warning theme is compared specifically for 16:28, while this proposed itinerary remains deferred.

case_assessments.current_assessment: No matching Melchi–Addi–Cosam–Elmadam–Er chain was established in the candidate genealogy. An Er elsewhere or the repeated Melchi inside Luke does not establish identity across these generations. The precise lineage remains deferred.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The Jesus-Eliezer-Jorim-Matthat-Levi chain was read. This ancestral Jesus is not identified with Jesus Christ, and repeated Levi or Matthat names elsewhere do not establish these links.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The ancestral Jesus–Eliezer–Jorim–Matthat–Levi sequence was distinguished from Jesus Christ and from other repeated Matthat or Levi names. The reread Matthew chain does not establish these links, so no identity-based target is retained.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The Simeon-Judah-Joseph-Jonam-Eliakim chain was read. No independent matching genealogy was established; familiar patriarchal names alone are insufficient for identity or relationship claims.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The Simeon–Judah–Joseph–Jonam–Eliakim sequence was read against the postexilic Matthew sequence. Neither familiar patriarchal names nor Matthew's differently situated Eliakim establishes the same persons or chain. No lineage harmonization receives credit.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The rolling, return and sitting after the scroll reading, with the congregation's fixed gaze, are distinctive scene details. No sufficiently specific separate counterpart was retained.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Nehemiah 8:5–8 provides a public Scripture reading and explanation, but has an opened book, standing audience and different actions. That shared setting does not add a specific counterpart to Jesus returning the rolled scroll, sitting, and receiving the synagogue's fixed gaze.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The physician proverb and anticipated demand to reproduce Capernaum's works in the homeland are distinctive to this exchange. Generic demands for signs or self-rescue were not counted as precise counterparts.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The physician-heal-yourself proverb anticipates a demand that Jesus demonstrate at home the works heard of elsewhere. At the cross the mockers similarly contrast His saving others with an alleged inability to save Himself. This compares the challenge to prove power on one's own behalf, with hometown demands and crucifixion mockery kept distinct; neither proverb nor mockery is endorsed as true.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The whole synagogue's anger at these particular prophetic examples has no sufficiently precise independent counterpart. A general offense or angry-crowd passage was not used as evidence of this reaction.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The synagogue becomes angry after Jesus' examples of aid to the Sidonian widow and the Syrian Naaman; Acts' crowd turns against Paul at the reported commission to Gentiles. Both scenes place a hostile response after speech about God's activity beyond Israel. The speakers, audiences, and occasions differ, and this does not reduce every listener's motives to an unstated explanation.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The expulsion from the city and attempted hurling from its hilltop are distinctive details. Other attempts on Jesus' life do not independently reproduce this method, place or sequence.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke's crowd takes Jesus outside the city and toward a hill to hurl Him down; Acts' crowd rushes Stephen and drives him outside the city to stone him. The concrete pattern is hostile collective expulsion for lethal violence. The persons, cities, methods, and outcomes differ; Stephen's stoning does not establish that Jesus was thrown from the hill.

case_assessments.previous_reason: Passing through the midst of this crowd and departing has no sufficiently specific retained counterpart. Other escapes from hostile groups were not merged with this event.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke says Jesus passes through the hostile crowd and departs; John says those seeking to seize Him do not retain Him and He goes out from their hand. These are distinct narrated escapes from hostile attempts to take Him. John does not reproduce the hilltop method, and neither account is used to add a miraculous mechanism or an identical occasion to the other.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The two boats at the shore, absent fishermen and washing of nets are distinctive observations. Other boat or net-work passages were not treated as independently reproducing all these circumstances.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke introduces fishermen's boats and nets being washed before Jesus' call; Mark introduces James and John in a boat putting the nets in order before their call. This compares fishing-work settings around the disciples' calling, while retaining washing versus putting in order and Luke's fishermen outside the boats versus Mark's named men in a boat.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The signal to partners, assistance from a second boat and both boats beginning to sink from the catch are distinctive. John's catch has a different sequence and does not state these details.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Both Jesus-directed catches produce so many fish that coordinated handling becomes necessary: Luke's partners bring the other boat and both boats become dangerously loaded, while John's disciples cannot draw the net and the others come in the little boat dragging it. John's scene is after the resurrection and says nothing about two boats sinking; the catches and handling sequences remain distinct.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The elders' specific claims that the centurion loves their nation and built their synagogue are not independently established by another retained passage. No other synagogue benefactor was identified with him.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke's elders commend their centurion's love for the nation and construction of their synagogue. Acts identifies Cornelius as a centurion who gives many alms to the people and prays continually. These are specific depictions of centurions' benefaction toward the people, not identification of the two men; Acts does not say Cornelius built Luke's synagogue.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The named journey to Nain with disciples and a large crowd has no sufficiently precise independent counterpart. Generic travel to a city was not used to manufacture one.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Jesus' journey to Nain introduces the following encounter with a widow whose son is restored; Elijah's journey to Zarephath brings him to a widow at the city gateway, before the later restoration of her son. This compares the opening movements in the wider widow-and-son narratives. The towns, time before the son's death, accompanying crowds, and manner of restoration are not equated.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The contrast between Simon's missing kiss and the woman's continuous kissing of Jesus' feet is distinctive. Other greeting kisses or anointing scenes do not reproduce this particular contrast.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The woman's repeated kisses of Jesus' feet are contrasted with Simon's omitted greeting kiss in this scene; Judas later approaches Jesus for a kiss and Jesus questions handing over the Son of Man with a kiss. These are contrasting uses of a kiss in Luke, devotion and hospitality versus betrayal, not the same kind of kiss, person, or incident.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The crowd's overwhelming amazement at God's majesty and the transition to Jesus' next prediction were read. Generic miracle amazement was not counted as a precise counterpart to this particular response and transition.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Mark 9:15 places the crowd's astonishment before the afflicted boy's healing, on seeing and greeting Jesus. Luke's response to God's majesty follows the healing and introduces another prediction. The timing and focus are distinct, and generic amazement alone is not retained.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The move to another village after the Samaritan rejection and rebuke was read. General travel or persecution-flight instructions do not independently reproduce this specific departure.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Matthew 10:23's instruction to flee persecution was compared with the Samaritan village's refusal and Jesus' subsequent departure. Luke does not describe flight from persecution here or reproduce the instruction; no punitive fire or extra departure detail is added.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The assault victim's Jerusalem-to-Jericho journey, stripping, beating and half-dead abandonment were read. No precise independent account of these story details was established; the mercy-story comparison is retained for the later aid actions instead.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The parable begins with a stripped, wounded traveler going toward Jericho; Chronicles describes naked, weakened captives being clothed, helped onto animals, and brought to Jericho. The wider mercy scenes share exposed vulnerability, aid, and Jericho, while the source of harm differs: robbery in Luke, captivity after war in Chronicles. No captive is identified as the parable's traveler.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The priest's chance arrival, seeing the victim and passing by were read. No independent counterpart establishes this action, and no ritual-purity motive for it is invented.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The priest sees a half-dead traveler on the road and passes by. Deuteronomy forbids seeing a brother's fallen donkey or calf in the way and disregarding it, requiring help instead. The law's explicit seeing-and-not-disregarding instruction supplies a bounded ethical contrast to passing the injured man; the animals and man are distinct, and no purity motive or knowledge of the priest's resources is invented.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The Levite's arrival, sight and passing by were read. His identity and motives are not derived from generic priestly or Levite regulations, and no close independent counterpart was established.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The Levite sees the injured traveler and passes by, whereas Proverbs commands rescue of people facing death and rejects ignorance of the person as an adequate excuse before God. This compares failure to aid a person in mortal need with the rescue instruction. Proverbs' people are being led to death, not victims of the same robbery; Luke does not state the Levite's motive.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The next-day two-denarii payment to the innkeeper and promised reimbursement were read. Unrelated payments or general hospitality commands do not reproduce these particular parable details.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The Samaritan personally guarantees repayment of further costs incurred caring for the injured man; Paul personally offers to have another's wrong or debt charged to him and promises repayment. The concrete connection is assuming another person's financial burden by an explicit repayment pledge. Innkeeper expenses and the possible debt concerning Onesimus differ, and neither pledge determines the other's amount.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The midnight friend's request to borrow three loaves was read. General bread petitions do not reproduce the friendship, hour or amount in this distinctive parable setup.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The friend-at-midnight story opens with a person asking another for needed help, and Luke11:8 explains persistence; the widow repeatedly petitions a judge who eventually responds because she troubles him. Both parables use persistent human requests in teaching about prayer. Friendship, bread, midnight and hospitality differ from an unjust judge and a demand for justice; God is not thereby identified as unwilling or unjust.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The arriving traveler and lack of food to set before him were read. General traveler-hospitality statements do not independently reproduce this friend's particular predicament.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke's traveler arrives at his friend's home, whose host has no food to offer; in Genesis evening travelers are invited into Lot's house and he prepares a feast and unleavened bread for them. This compares the concrete responsibility of receiving travelers with food and shelter. Lot's angelic visitors and available provision are not inserted into Luke's friend or his lack of bread.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The shut door, children in bed and initial refusal to rise were read. No close independent counterpart establishes these details, and unrelated closed-door stories are not substituted.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The man inside initially refuses the midnight request, invoking the shut door and children in bed; Luke's judge is initially unwilling but later yields to the widow's repeated troubling. With Luke 11:8 supplying the first story's eventual response, the comparison concerns resistance overcome by persistence. Household inconvenience and the judge's stated character are different reasons, not proof that the friend is the same unjust figure.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The law expert's response that Jesus' words insult his group was read. Generic offense reactions do not independently reproduce this speaker and intervention.
case_assessments.current_assessment: An expert in the Law tells Jesus that His rebuke insults his group; Matthew's disciples report that the Pharisees stumbled at His saying in a dispute that also begins with handwashing traditions. This compares religious interlocutors' adverse reception of Jesus' purity-related correction. The reporter, wording, teaching sequence and occasion differ; the passages do not independently reproduce the same objection.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The particular request that Jesus compel a brother to divide an inheritance was read. General inheritance rules do not establish this claimant's rights or circumstances, so no independent counterpart was retained.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Deuteronomy 21:15–17 regulates paternal inheritance and the firstborn's portion, but the claimant's birth rank, family structure and legal rights are unspecified. Unlike the father's division scene in Luke 15:12, this request gives no particular basis for applying that provision. It remains deferred.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The rich man's question about insufficient crop storage was read. No sufficiently precise counterpart to that particular deliberation was retained.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Both parables give an economic protagonist's private deliberation in the form 'What shall I do?' followed by the difficulty he faces and a plan. The rich man has too much produce to store, while the steward is losing his position and fears digging or begging. This is a specific repeated monologue pattern, not the same predicament or a common approval of the plans.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The plan to demolish and enlarge storehouses was read. Other accounts of storing grain were not treated as this same demolition-and-rebuilding plan.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke's rich man plans larger storehouses to gather abundant grain and his goods; Genesis describes abundant years and Joseph gathering their food into the cities. The concrete comparison is organized grain storage after agricultural abundance. Joseph's preceding plan preserves the land through famine, unlike the rich man's self-directed security; Genesis supplies neither demolition of barns nor Luke's promised years of personal ease.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The report of Pilate mixing Galileans' blood with their sacrifices was read. No independent biblical account of this specific event was established.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Psalm 78:1–3 was considered for violent bloodshed and violation of worship. It describes foreign devastation of Jerusalem, not Pilate's Galileans or blood mixed with their sacrifices. The common religious-violence topic is not retained as a sufficiently particular comparison.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The eighteen tower deaths at Siloam were read. Generic tower or disaster passages do not independently establish this event or its victims.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Jesus' question challenges the assumption that the Siloam victims were greater debtors than their neighbors; John's disciples ask whose sin caused a man's congenital blindness, and Jesus rejects their proposed individual-or-parental explanation. Both passages resist a simple inference from suffering to exceptional personal guilt. John does not attest the tower deaths, and neither passage declares everyone morally sinless.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The bent woman's eighteen-year spirit of weakness was read. Other chronic illnesses do not independently attest this distinctive condition or duration.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The later saying explicitly returns to this woman and the same eighteen years, describing her as a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound and whose bond ought to be released. It interprets the earlier spirit of weakness within this particular healing controversy. This is an internal explanatory reference, not an independent diagnosis or a rule that every chronic illness has the same cause.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The particular call and pronouncement of release to this woman were read. Generic healing pronouncements were not used solely to complete the unit.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Jesus pronounces the woman released from her weakness; His earlier synagogue proclamation announces release to captives and to the oppressed. The following Sabbath argument explicitly describes this woman's release from bondage. This is a narrative illustration of the announced release motif, not a claim that every expression in the earlier proclamation denotes this woman's condition or that the pronouncement is a direct quotation.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The Pharisees' warning that Herod wanted to kill Jesus was read. Other Herod notices were not treated as independent confirmation of this specific warning or its truth.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Both scenes contain an instruction to leave because Herod seeks Jesus' life. Matthew's angel addresses Joseph about the Child and an Egyptian refuge, while Luke records Pharisees warning the adult Jesus, whose reply follows. The life stages, speakers and Herod settings are distinct; the comparison neither identifies the Herods nor establishes that Jesus fled in response to the Pharisees.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The fox reply and today/tomorrow/third-day completion wording were read. It was not simply equated with a separately stated resurrection timetable or a generic healing summary.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Jesus tells messengers to report His healings in both scenes: to John after works including deliverance from evil spirits, and to the ruler described as a fox with a declaration of ongoing exorcisms and healings. The recipient, tone and setting differ. Luke 7 does not explain the fox epithet or the today/tomorrow/third-day completion language, which is not silently equated with a resurrection timetable.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The man with dropsy was read. Other sick men or Sabbath healings do not independently attest this distinct illness and appearance.
case_assessments.current_assessment: A man with dropsy stands before Jesus during a Sabbath meal under close observation; Mark introduces a man with a withered hand in the synagogue while observers watch for a Sabbath healing to accuse Him. These are specific Sabbath-healing controversy settings with different patients, ailments and venues. Mark does not independently attest dropsy or identify its patient as Luke's man.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The servant's statement that the order was completed while room remained was read. The different banquet story's final fullness was not retained as an exact counterpart to this progress report.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Both banquet parables report the result of servants gathering people beyond the original invitees. Luke's slave says the command is fulfilled but room remains, prompting another outreach; Matthew says the wedding feast is filled after gathering people from the roads. This compares the reports and their differing stages, preserving remaining capacity versus fullness rather than replacing Luke's statement with Matthew's.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The traveling crowd and Jesus' turning to address it were read. Generic crowd and travel transitions were not used to manufacture a counterpart.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke describes Jesus addressing the great crowd traveling with Him before the cross-bearing demands of discipleship; Mark explicitly calls the crowd together with the disciples to hear self-denial and cross-bearing instruction. The connection is the public audience and introduction to the same costly-following theme. Being already on the road and being summoned are distinct narrative arrangements, not an identical occasion asserted.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The unfinished foundation and resulting mockery were read. Mockery of other building projects does not establish this precise failure from insufficient resources.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The uncompleted building brings spectators' mockery in Luke; Nehemiah records opponents laughing at the Jews' wall building and deriding the wall's strength before a prayer about becoming an object of mockery. This is a concrete construction-and-ridicule comparison. Nehemiah's opponents do not establish an actual abandonment for lack of funds, and their wall is not Luke's tower.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The spectators' statement about beginning but not finishing was read. No sufficiently precise independent counterpart was retained.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke's hypothetical builder begins but cannot finish; Zechariah promises that the hands of Zerubbabel which laid the house's foundation will complete it. The contrast concerns beginning and completing a building, with human cost calculation in Luke and a prophetic assurance in Zechariah. No identical project or general promise to complete every undertaking is inferred.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The younger son's demand and the father's division of livelihood were read. A presumed legal share, firstborn ratio, or identical family dispute was not supplied from general inheritance passages.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The father divides property between his sons after the younger requests his share; Deuteronomy regulates a father's assignment of possessions to sons and protects the firstborn's double portion. This is legal background to a paternal inheritance division, not proof of the precise shares or timing in the parable. Luke does not supply the law's two-wives situation or explicitly calculate either son's portion.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The famine after the son's spending was read. Other famines do not independently attest these circumstances or establish the same country.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Ruth 1:1–6 was read for famine, loss abroad and return toward food. Its famine precedes migration, while Luke's famine follows the son's journey and spending. The shared hardship setting does not add a close connection to this sequence or identify the country, so no pair is retained.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The son's employment feeding pigs was read. Purity laws about eating pork were not represented as an explicit law about this job, and unrelated herdsmen do not establish his identity.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke places the needy son in work feeding pigs; Leviticus classifies the pig as unclean for Israel and prohibits eating its flesh or touching its carcass. This provides a specific scriptural background for the animal in the scene. It does not turn a dietary and carcass rule into an express prohibition on this employment or assert that the son ate pork.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The carob-pod hunger and nobody giving him anything were read. No sufficiently precise separate counterpart was retained.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The hungry son longs to be filled with the pigs' food and receives nothing; the poor man at the rich man's gate longs to be filled with what falls from the table. Both nearby parables depict unfulfilled food longing beside abundance and animals. The pigs eat pods, while the dogs lick sores; Luke does not say the dogs eat the table scraps or identify the two hungry men.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The internal comparison of the father's workers' bread with his hunger was read. General bread or hunger sayings were not treated as this particular realization.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The father's later provision of clothing and a calf feast was compared with the son's thought about hired workers' abundant bread. It answers his deprivation generally but does not repeat the workers' position or this specific realization. No generic bread or hunger link is added.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The older son hearing music and dancing on returning from the field was read. Other musical scenes do not establish this distinctive approach to the house.
case_assessments.current_assessment: An approaching person hears a celebration and then reacts angrily in each wider scene: Luke's older son hears music and dancing before resenting his brother's welcome; Joshua and Moses hear camp sounds, and Moses sees dancing and becomes angry. The limited narrative comparison preserves a legitimate family celebration versus idolatrous revelry; no idolatry or moral approval of the brother's anger is imported into Luke.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The older son's question to a servant was read. Generic questions about noises or crowds were not retained as close counterparts.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Luke 18:36–37 also narrates hearing something, asking what it means, and receiving a report. That is a common inquiry pattern with different hearers, sounds and consequences; it offers no stronger substantive connection to the older son's particular servant question.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The steward's private deliberation about digging and begging after dismissal was read. Generic economic worries do not repeat this particular dilemma.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The steward and rich man each reason privately with 'What shall I do?' and name an economic difficulty before proposing a solution. The steward faces removal and inability or reluctance to do other work; the rich man faces crop-storage capacity. The recurring deliberation formula connects the parables without making their circumstances, motives, plans or ensuing evaluations identical.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The calling of the master's debtors and first debt question were read. No precise independent counterpart to this negotiation was retained.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The steward summons his master's debtors and asks the first what he owes; Matthew's king begins settling accounts and a deeply indebted servant is brought before him. Both parables stage obligations owed to a master through an accounting encounter. The steward is an intermediary, whereas the king is the creditor; debt amounts and the actions that follow are different.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The hundred-to-fifty oil-document revision was read. A theory about removing interest or commission was not invented, and other debts do not independently establish these figures.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The two consecutive transactions deliberately repeat the debt question and written-document revision while changing commodity and figures: a hundred baths of oil becomes fifty here, and a hundred kors of wheat becomes eighty in the second. This is an internal structural comparison of the steward's dealings. The different reductions do not establish an interest-rate, commission, or legally authorized remission theory.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The hundred-to-eighty wheat-document revision was read. No unverified commercial explanation or independent validation of these figures was supplied.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The wheat transaction repeats the earlier oil debtor's written revision, but changes a hundred to eighty rather than a hundred to fifty. This explicit repeated transaction pattern permits comparison of the different stated reductions without treating the commodities or quantities as identical. No explanation involving removed interest, commission, local prices, or the master's authorization is added.

case_assessments.previous_reason: Lazarus's poverty, gateway location, and sores were read. General sore-covered sufferers were not treated as this figure or a sufficiently precise separate account.
case_assessments.current_assessment: Job 2:7–8 was read for bodily sores and a sufferer outside an ordinary residential setting. Job's ulcer, its stated cause and dung-heap scene differ from Lazarus's unnamed cause and placement at the rich man's gate. The general afflicted-person resemblance remains too loose for a retained pair.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The plea for a wet finger to cool the tongue in flame was read. Generic thirst or fire texts were not retained as an exact counterpart to this distinctive request.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The formerly feasting rich man asks for water in painful torment while Lazarus is comforted in the surrounding dialogue. Isaiah contrasts the Lord's servants eating, drinking and rejoicing with opponents' hunger, thirst and cries of heart-pain. This is a bounded judgment-and-reversal comparison, not a source for the wet-finger request, flame mechanism, or an identical map of the afterlife.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The fixed, uncrossable chasm was read. No independent matching passage was established, and extra geography was not added.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The fixed chasm prevents movement between torment and Abraham's company; the earlier teaching depicts a closed door, rejected pleas to enter, and people outside seeing Abraham in God's kingdom. Both depict decisive exclusion alongside awareness of Abraham's blessed company. Chasm and doorway remain different images, with no claim that the scenes give identical geography or add a later crossing possibility.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The request to send Lazarus to the father's house was read. No independent counterpart to this particular proposed visit was retained.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The proposed visit to the father's house was reread with Abraham's reply and the request's warning purpose. The reply interprets the same dialogue rather than supplying a separate visit, and no actual journey by a dead messenger is inferred. The warning theme is compared specifically for 16:28, while this proposed itinerary remains deferred.

case_assessments.previous_reason: The five brothers and requested warning were read. They were not assigned names, historical relatives, or a symbolic identification without evidence.
case_assessments.current_assessment: The rich man wants his living brothers solemnly warned so they may avoid torment; Ezekiel's watchman must convey God's warning so a lawless hearer may turn and live rather than die. The connection is warning before destructive judgment with an opportunity to change. Ezekiel neither identifies the five brothers nor authorizes a visit from the dead; the following Luke dialogue instead points to Moses and the Prophets.

review_notes: All 75 previously deferred Luke source units in chapters 1–16 were reread with their actual narrative or speech context. Proposed comparisons are substantive reconsiderations rather than new first readings; unretained cases continue to receive zero completion credit.

49 source units have one proposed pair each; 26 remain deferred. The proposals include bounded analogies, contrasts, legal background, repeated literary forms and explicit same-book explanations, rather than requiring every unit to have an independent duplicate of all details.

Internal links expressly identify their function: retrospective explanation of an earlier action, contrast with an earlier command, repeated economic deliberation, repeated debt transactions, or interpretation of a particular healing. They are not independent witnesses or additional events.

The possible Samuel visitation echo is qualified as a journey-pattern comparison and does not identify Mary with the ark or settle the city. Kings' prophetess is named Olda in this supplied text; her role does not establish Anna's identity or biography.

Chronological registration notices are compared without equating Luke's census with Judas's registration or resolving the Quirinius issue. Repeated genealogical names remain uncredited where no matching chain establishes the persons and relationships.

Distinct Herod scenes, escapes, Sabbath patients, infant visitors, widow narratives and fishing catches retain different life stages, places, actions and outcomes. Neither allusion nor partial comparison silently combines their sequences.

Inheritance and pig-law references provide limited textual background; they do not establish a particular share, a firstborn ratio for Luke's family, an age-twelve ceremony, a prohibition on feeding pigs, or an assertion that the son ate pork.

Nehemiah's construction mockery uses actual original IDs 3:33–36. Comparisons with Zechariah's completion promise preserve an opposite outcome and do not promise success for every proposed building project.

Reversal and judgment parallels preserve different images and speakers without adding afterlife geography, identifying Lazarus with another person, or assigning names or symbolism to the five brothers. No interest or commission theory explains the steward's different reductions.

Each case preserves its old reason and SHA-256 of the exact UTF-8 source text, with the new assessment separately recorded. Source wording, divisions, original gaps, IDs and continuation bodies remain unchanged.

Retained target IDs and their contiguous original order, exact 75-case coverage, source/target exclusion and directed-pair uniqueness are checked before final handoff. This is English passage review, not an exhaustive concordance or fresh specialist approval of a critical text.
